name: Omar Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brightline Connect, an outsourcing firm that runs the customer lines for a big mobile phone network. We're in an old printworks by the canal, about two hundred of us on the floor. My day is half calls and half chats, mostly people who've gone over their data, want to cancel, or whose new phone hasn't arrived. I like the cancellation calls, oddly, because you can sometimes talk someone into a better deal and they leave happier.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how do you get on with the tech?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Five years at Brightline, two of them as one of the go-to people for retention. I live with my girlfriend Lena, she's a nursery nurse, in a rented flat near the station, and we've got about four months saved. I use the AI summary button now and then when a chat gets long, but only once I saw it actually got the account notes right. Thursdays I play five-a-side, that's my sanity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically what I've seen so far, to be fair. The summary button's handy, but it's not running the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd joke that the robot uprising got cancelled. Online I'd say the real story is how outsourcers squeeze pay, AI or not. I'd probably repost something from the union about call centre conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be a bit on edge, because our whole floor lives on a contract. The phone network renews with Brightline every two years, and if someone offshore bids lower, we're gone, no AI needed. So nothing changing doesn't mean I'm safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and use the summary tool where it helps. I'd keep the savings ticking over, about sixty a month. I'd also finally join the union, because a couple of mates on the floor keep asking me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine day to day. Slightly tense around renewal time, which is next March. It's the usual kind of worry, not a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on the floor around renewal time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone gets quiet and the team leaders get very keen on our numbers. Last renewal they cut the bonus scheme to win the contract, so we paid for it in our wages. I'd expect the same thing next March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the bonus went again, what would you and Lena change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd drop the second streaming service and I'd stop buying lunch from the café by the canal. Lena's pay is steady but small, so mine is the one that wobbles. We wouldn't touch the savings unless something broke.

say: I'd joke that the **robot uprising** got cancelled.
I'd say outsourcers **squeeze pay** whether AI works or not, and share union posts.
think: Our floor lives on a **two-year contract** that could go offshore anytime.
Nothing changing **doesn't mean safe** when the bonus already got cut once.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** only where it saves time on long chats.
Keep saving **sixty a month** and finally join the union.
feel: He feels **fine day to day**, with tension around the March renewal.
S0.quote: The phone network renews with Brightline every two years, and if someone offshore bids lower, we're gone, no AI needed.
fieldNote: His worry comes from **outsourcing contracts**, not from the technology.
He's already lost a **bonus scheme** once to win a renewal.
He uses AI only once it's **proven useful**, true to his steady style.

steps.text: Keep handling retention calls and use the summary button on long chats
Keep saving sixty a month into the joint account
Join the union branch at the Brightline floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers, coding, booking, yeah. That's the network's whole help section turned into a bot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that firms should share the savings with the people they keep, and retrain the ones they don't. I'd be loud about it online, especially about outsourcers. At work I'd tell the younger lads to learn the new tools, because refusing won't save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Brightline loses half the floor within two years. The easy calls go to the bot, and Brightline keeps a smaller team for angry customers and cancellations. I reckon I'd be in that smaller team, but I'm not certain, and my pay would probably drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of people on the floor were using the new system well, then copy what works. I'd take the retention-specialist training if Brightline offered it, so I'm in the team they keep. I'd push savings to a hundred a month and go to union meetings about how the cuts are chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I don't feel helpless. I've seen this kind of thing before with self-service apps. It feels like a squeeze rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the floor would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sanjay, who's twenty and only does the data top-up queue. That's exactly what a bot does best. He's got no savings and still lives with his mum, so I'd make sure he knows about the union and the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your pay would probably drop even if you kept your seat. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the kept team would do the hardest calls all day, but there'd be fewer bonuses to hand out. Brightline always finds a way to make the contract cheaper. More stress for the same money, maybe less.

I'd tell younger colleagues to **learn the tools**, because refusing won't save them.

steps.text: Learn the new bot-handover system once teammates show it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's different. That's not a squeeze, that's the whole building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to act now, with real money, not a website about retraining. I'd join the protests and I'd tell everyone online that nobody voted for this. At work I'd stop telling people to learn the tools, because there'd be no tools left to learn, just the AI itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect Brightline to close the floor within a year of 2028. Every single thing I do is talking and typing. The three years before robots only help people whose jobs use their hands, so I'd need to become one of those people fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at trades with Lena that week. Her brother is an electrician and he's said before he could get me on as a mate on his jobs. I'd cut the café lunches and the streaming, save every spare penny, and start evening classes in electrical installation within a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Then a bit numb. I think I'd be short with Lena and not mean to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Electrical work gets robots about 2031 in this picture. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, but three years of wages is three years of wages. And rewiring an old house is the sort of thing robots would take ages to get right. I'd rather bet on old houses than on a headset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'd be poorer for a while, maybe a year on apprentice money. She'd be fine with it, she's practical. I'd worry more about telling my mum, who was so proud I had an office job.

say: I'd say the government must act with **real money**, not a retraining website.
I'd join **protests** and say online that nobody voted for this.
think: Brightline closes the floor **within a year** of AGI arriving.
Robots coming later only help **hands-on jobs**, so I'd need to switch fast.

Start **evening classes** in electrical installation within a few months.

S2.quote: I'd rather bet on old houses than on a headset.
fieldNote: He moves quickly once the threat is **unmistakable**, despite usually waiting.
Lena's brother gives him a **real route** into hands-on work.
His mum's **pride** in his office job is an emotional hurdle.

steps.text: Start evening classes in electrical installation
Work as an electrician's mate for Lena's brother
Drop café lunches and the second streaming service
Join protests calling for government money for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to do it properly, I think, if I don't sit on my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should start now and not wait for the company to tell them. I'd tell the union to push Brightline for paid study leave. Online I'd keep banging on about outsourcers being first to dump staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have about three years at Brightline before it really bites, and I'd use them. Thinking work goes in 2031 and hands-on goes later, so I want to be in something practical by then. I'd still wait a year to see which trades are actually holding up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and use the AI tools more, so I stay useful until the end. In year two I'd start the electrical course part-time. We'd keep saving and probably stay renting rather than buy, so we can move if the work is somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a plan in it. It feels like a job I have to do rather than a disaster. Some nights it'd still get me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year to see which trades hold up. Isn't that time you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I've seen mates jump into crypto courses and coding bootcamps and lose money, so I'd rather be second in than first and wrong. One year of watching is fine with five years on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lena change anything in your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on buying, definitely. Lena's nursery job is hands-on, so hers might outlast mine. We'd probably plan around her work instead of mine, which is a funny thought.

I'd push the union to win **paid study leave** from Brightline.

He'd keep renting to stay **mobile** for work.

steps.text: Use Brightline's AI tools more to stay on the kept team
Start a part-time electrical course in the second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That feels like a long runway, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this fairly, so let's do it fairly. I'd want the union and the government making plans for call centre workers specifically. Online I'd be less angry and more practical about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably stay at Brightline a good while longer. I'd keep an eye on things and move when I see the floor start to shrink. Ten years is enough for me to switch once, properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing retention calls and use whatever AI tools come in. I'd save steadily and maybe start the electrical course around year four or five. Lena and I would likely buy a small place in the next few years, since we wouldn't be rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. There's a little alarm bell, but it's quiet. It's background noise rather than a siren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move when you see the floor shrink. What would be the sign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Brightline stops replacing people who leave, that's always the first sign the floor is shrinking. Then the team leaders start talking about efficiency in every huddle. When that happens I'd sign up for the course the same month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sanjay, still. He's young enough to switch, but he won't think about it until it's too late. I'd nag him about it every Friday until he got sick of me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I do is talking and typing, and two years isn't enough to learn a trade. What would help is paid training while you're still on wages, and outsourcers being made to give proper notice instead of losing a contract and closing the floor in a month.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the people who outsource us. The phone network will say it never sacked anyone, because technically we work for Brightline. Somebody should have to own what happens to us.

headlineQuote: The phone network will say it never sacked anyone, because technically we work for Brightline.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** retention agent at Brightline Connect, an outsourcer for a mobile network.
He lives with **Lena**, a nursery nurse, and they have about **four months** saved.
He uses AI **only once it's proven** and prefers to be second in rather than first.
In the fast AGI picture he'd move into **electrical work** through Lena's brother.
He blames **outsourcing** as much as AI, and wants someone to own the fallout.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is all talking and typing with no time to learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: Outsourcers forced to give **proper notice** before closing a floor.
